warmup.q: A payment service has slow authorizations every few minutes. Your logs say "issuer call took 230 ms" for those requests. What can a JFR recording of the same minutes tell you that the log line can't?
options: Nothing more: the log already has the duration
Whether a GC pause, a lock wait or a burst of allocation happened at the same moments, on the same timeline
The SQL plan of every query
warmup.why: JFR records the JVM's own events (GC pauses, monitor waits, allocation and CPU samples, compilations) with timestamps and threads, next to any events you add. So you can see what else was happening when the slow call ran. It can't see inside the issuer, and SQL plans live in the database.

sections.h: JFR records what the JVM was doing, and it's already in your JDK
sections.html:
Start with the problem. Authorizations are sometimes slow. The hand-made fix is a timer and a log line: log.info("issuer call took {} ms", ms). That gives you one number per call. It doesn't tell you whether a garbage collection paused every thread at that moment, whether the thread waited for a lock, or whether the code allocated 2 GB that second.

JDK Flight Recorder (JFR) is a recorder built into HotSpot. It writes events, small timestamped records, about what the JVM is doing: GC pauses, JIT compilations, threads waiting on locks, sampled stacks of running threads (execution samples), sampled allocations, file and socket I/O, and more. Your own code can add events too. Everything lands in one timeline, in a compact binary format, kept in memory buffers and written to disk.

You start a recording from the command line or on a live JVM:

java -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=rec.jfr,settings=profile -jar app.jar

jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=pay settings=profile    # attach to a running JVM
jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=pay filename=pay.jfr     # copy what it has so far to a file
jcmd <pid> JFR.stop name=pay

The JVM answers with real lines like these (JDK 21):

Started recording 1. No limit specified, using maxsize=250MB as default.
Use jcmd 4971 JFR.dump name=1 to copy recording data to file.

With filename= set, the file is written when the JVM exits. settings picks a configuration file. default.jfc is meant to stay on. profile.jfc, in the words of the java man page, "provides more data than the default configuration, but can have more overhead", so use it for shorter periods. The difference is in the details. In JDK 25, default samples thread stacks every 20 ms and allocations at up to 150 per second, and records lock waits of 20 ms or more. profile samples every 10 ms, records up to 300 allocation samples a second, and records lock waits from 10 ms.

try.title: Record a busy payment service
steps: Read JfrDemo and skim PaymentWorkload next to it: four threads compute fees with BigDecimal, call a fake issuer that sleeps, and sometimes hold a shared lock for 15 ms.
Predict which event type will be the most common in the recording.
Run it. The demo starts a second JVM with -XX:StartFlightRecording and prints the path of the .jfr file.
Run jfr summary on that file (the demo prints the command).

code.title: JfrDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l05; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Runs PaymentWorkload for 4 seconds in a second JVM started with * -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=build/perf05.jfr,settings=profile * and tells you where the recording is. */ public class JfrDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { PaymentWorkload.run(4); return; } Path file = Path.of("build", "perf05.jfr").toAbsolutePath(); String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), JfrDemo.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).inheritIO().start(); p.waitFor(); System.out.println("recording written to " + file); System.out.println("try: jfr summary " + file); } }

alt.title: JfrDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l05 import jdk.jfr.Category import jdk.jfr.Description import jdk.jfr.Event import jdk.jfr.Label import jdk.jfr.Name import java.math.BigDecimal import java.math.RoundingMode import java.nio.file.Path import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of JfrDemo.java (with its workload and event in this one file). It runs the workload // for 4 seconds in a second JVM started with -XX:StartFlightRecording and writes build/perf05-kt.jfr. @Name("workbench.IssuerCall") @Label("Issuer Call") @Category("Workbench", "Payments") @Description("A call to the card issuer during authorization") class KIssuerCallEvent : Event() { @Label("Merchant") var merchant: String? = null // a Kotlin property: JFR records its field @Label("Amount (cents)") var amountCents = 0L @Label("Approved") var approved = false } private val ledger = Any() fun kFee(amount: String): Long = (BigDecimal(amount) * BigDecimal("0.029")).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN).unscaledValue().toLong() fun kCallIssuer(merchant: String, cents: Long): Boolean { val event = KIssuerCallEvent() event.begin() Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(2, if (merchant == "m_7") 40 else 12).toLong()) val approved = cents < 400_000 event.end() if (event.shouldCommit()) { // skip the field work when no recording wants it event.merchant = merchant event.amountCents = cents event.approved = approved event.commit() } return approved } fun kRunWorkload(seconds: Int) { val until = System.nanoTime() + seconds * 1_000_000_000L val workers = (0 until 4).map { w -> thread(name = "auth-$w") { var sink = 0L var i = 0 while (System.nanoTime() < until) { for (k in 0 until 2_000) sink += kFee("${100 + (k + i) % 9_000}.25") kCallIssuer("m_${i % 10}", 1_000 + (i * 7_919L) % 500_000) if (i % 25 == w) synchronized(ledger) { Thread.sleep(15) } // a ledger write under a shared lock i++ } if (sink == 42L) println() } } workers.forEach { it.join() } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") return kRunWorkload(4) val file = Path.of("build", "perf05-kt.jfr").toAbsolutePath() val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=$file,settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l05.JfrDemoKt", "child") .inheritIO().start().waitFor() println("recording written to $file") println("try: jfr summary $file") }

try.expect: The JVM prints the two "Started recording" lines, then the demo prints the file path, about 400 KB after 4 seconds. In one run, jfr summary listed 1,746 workbench.IssuerCall events (the demo's own), 1,126 jdk.ObjectAllocationSample, 960 jdk.GCPhaseParallel and 530 jdk.ThreadSleep, but only 28 jdk.ExecutionSample, because the threads spend most of their time sleeping.

sections.h: Ask the recording questions with jfr summary, view and print
sections.html:
The jfr tool ships with the JDK. Three of its subcommands cover most days.

jfr summary rec.jfr lists every event type with its count and size. Read it first, to see what the recording holds.

jfr view <view> rec.jfr prints a ready-made report. It arrived in JDK 21 with 74 views, and JDK 25 has 83. The ones you'll use most are hot-methods, allocation-by-site, gc-pauses, contention-by-site and deoptimizations-by-reason (lesson 2's uncommon traps, counted). Real output from the demo's recording:

                     Contention by Site

StackTrace                                                    Count    Avg.    Max.
------------------------------------------------------------- ----- ------- -------
workbench.performance.l05.PaymentWorkload.authorizeLoop(int,      7 15.5 ms 25.0 ms

                     Allocation by Site

Method                                                  Allocation Pressure
------------------------------------------------------- -------------------
workbench.performance.l05.PaymentWorkload.fee(String)               40.82%
java.lang.StringLatin1.toChars(byte[])                              26.97%

Each view is a query over events. jfr view --verbose allocation-by-site rec.jfr shows the columns it sums, and the JDK source defines it as SELECT stackTrace.topFrame AS S, SUM(weight) AS W FROM ObjectAllocationSample GROUP BY S ORDER BY W DESC. You can also pass an event type as the view, such as jfr view workbench.IssuerCall rec.jfr, and get a table of those events. On a live JVM, jcmd <pid> JFR.view hot-methods prints the same report without dumping a file (it works on JDK 21 as well).

jfr print --events workbench.IssuerCall --stack-depth 2 rec.jfr prints events one by one, with every field and a short stack trace. Add --json for something a script can read.

JDK Mission Control (JMC) is the desktop app for the same files: timelines, flame graphs of the samples, and automated analysis. It's developed in the openjdk/jmc project and downloaded separately from builds that several vendors publish. The jfr tool is enough for everything in this lesson.

One warning before you send a recording to anyone. The demo's recording also holds 169 jdk.InitialEnvironmentVariable events and the full command line. For a payment service that can mean secrets. JDK 27 adds in-process redaction (JEP 536, -XX:FlightRecorderOptions:redact-argument=...). On older JDKs, check what's in the file first.

sections.h: Your own events put business context on the same timeline
sections.html:
A JFR event is a class that extends jdk.jfr.Event. Its fields are the data. Annotations give it a stable name and labels for the tools:

Java
@Name("workbench.IssuerCall")
@Label("Issuer Call")
@Category({"Workbench", "Payments"})
public class IssuerCallEvent extends Event {
    @Label("Merchant") String merchant;
    @Label("Amount (cents)") long amountCents;
    @Label("Approved") boolean approved;
}

IssuerCallEvent event = new IssuerCallEvent();
event.begin();                                  // 1. start the clock
boolean approved = issuer.approve(merchant, cents);
event.end();                                    // 2. stop it
if (event.shouldCommit()) {                     // 3. false if no recording wants it
    event.merchant = merchant;
    event.amountCents = cents;
    event.approved = approved;
    event.commit();                             // 4. write it, with a stack trace
}
Kotlin
@Name("workbench.IssuerCall")
@Label("Issuer Call")
@Category("Workbench", "Payments")
class KIssuerCallEvent : Event() {
    @Label("Merchant") var merchant: String? = null
    @Label("Amount (cents)") var amountCents = 0L
    @Label("Approved") var approved = false
}

val event = KIssuerCallEvent()
event.begin()                                   // 1. start the clock
val approved = issuer.approve(merchant, cents)
event.end()                                     // 2. stop it
if (event.shouldCommit()) {                     // 3. false if no recording wants it
    event.merchant = merchant
    event.amountCents = cents
    event.approved = approved
    event.commit()                              // 4. write it, with a stack trace
}

begin() and end() give the event its duration. commit() writes it, with the thread and a stack trace taken at that moment. shouldCommit() returns true only if some recording has the event enabled and the duration passes that recording's threshold, so you can skip filling in fields nobody will read. Kotlin needs nothing special: JFR records the fields behind Kotlin properties, and @Label on a property lands on the field.

Compared with the log line from the first section, the event is structured (fields, not text to parse), off unless a recording asks for it, and filterable per recording: -XX:StartFlightRecording:+workbench.IssuerCall#threshold=30ms,... keeps only calls of 30 ms or more. The + is needed because your event isn't listed in the .jfc file. Without it, the JVM warns that the setting "doesn't exist" and ignores it. Above all, it sits on the same timeline as the GC pauses and lock waits, with the same thread names.

The demo's events, as jfr view workbench.IssuerCall shows them:

Start Time Duration Event Thread Stack Trace                                            Merchant Amount (cents) Approved
---------- -------- ------------ ------------------------------------------------------ -------- -------------- --------
18:05:59    9.94 ms auth-3       workbench.performance.l05.PaymentWorkload.callIssuer   m_0               1,000     true
18:05:59    3.37 ms auth-2       workbench.performance.l05.PaymentWorkload.callIssuer   m_0               1,000     true

Reading events back in code is short. RecordingFile.readAllEvents(path) returns every event, and each RecordedEvent has getEventType().getName(), getDuration(), getString("merchant"), getBoolean("approved") and friends. That's the lab.

Check yourself: you commit an event in a method that runs 50,000 times a second, and no recording enables it. What does shouldCommit() return, and what does it save you? (False. It saves the work of filling in the fields, and commit() would write nothing anyway.)

try.title: Keep only the slow calls
steps: In JfrDemo.java, change the recording option to "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile,+workbench.IssuerCall#threshold=30ms" (note the +).
Predict: out of about 1,700 issuer calls, roughly how many will be recorded now?
Run the demo again, then jfr summary and jfr view workbench.IssuerCall on the new file.
try.expect: Only a few dozen workbench.IssuerCall events remain (43 in one run, against 1,744 without the threshold), all from m_7 and all 30 ms or longer, because only that merchant's fake issuer sleeps that long. The JVM's own events are unchanged. The threshold is a setting of the recording, not of your code.

sections.h: Stream events live, and what JDK 25 added
sections.html:
A recording file answers questions after the fact. jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingStream, available since JDK 14, delivers the same events to your code while the JVM runs:

Java
try (RecordingStream rs = new RecordingStream()) {
    rs.enable("workbench.IssuerCall").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(35));
    rs.onEvent("workbench.IssuerCall", e -> System.out.printf("slow issuer call: %s, %d ms%n",
            e.getString("merchant"), e.getDuration().toMillis()));
    rs.startAsync();                 // events arrive on a background thread
    PaymentWorkload.run(3);
}
Kotlin
RecordingStream().use { rs ->
    rs.enable("workbench.IssuerCall").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(35))
    rs.onEvent("workbench.IssuerCall") { e ->
        println("slow issuer call: ${e.getString("merchant")}, ${e.duration.toMillis()} ms")
    }
    rs.startAsync()                  // events arrive on a background thread
    kRunWorkload(3)
}

That's enough to turn JVM events into metrics or alerts inside the service, for example GC pause time per minute. Events arrive in batches after a short delay, so this is monitoring, not a callback on the hot path.

JDK 25 added three profiling features. All of these ran here on JDK 25:

  • Method timing and tracing (JEP 520). -XX:StartFlightRecording:method-timing=Work::fee,report-on-exit=method-timing counted and timed one method with no code change. It printed 21,282,793 invocations, an average of 0.000063 ms and a maximum of 7.54 ms. The filter can also be an annotation such as @jakarta.ws.rs.GET.
  • CPU-time sampling (JEP 509), experimental and Linux only. Enable jdk.CPUTimeSample (for example jdk.CPUTimeSample#enabled=true,jdk.CPUTimeSample#throttle=10ms) and read it with jfr view cpu-time-hot-methods. It samples each thread by the CPU time it uses. In a 3-second run of one busy thread at 10 ms, it collected 276 samples, close to the 300 you'd expect.
  • Cooperative sampling (JEP 518) changes how the JVM takes execution samples internally. You don't configure it.

report-on-exit=<view> itself is also there in JDK 25 (JDK 21 rejects it), and it prints any view when the JVM exits: a profile in your CI log for free.

try.title: Watch slow calls and GCs as they happen
steps: Run StreamingDemo and watch the output for 3 seconds.
Predict before running the Kotlin twin: which merchant will show up, and roughly how slow?
On JDK 25 only: run the workload with method timing, using the command in the note below, and compare the printed table with your expectations.

code.title: StreamingDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l05; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingStream; import java.time.Duration; /** Watches the running JVM with JFR event streaming: slow issuer calls and garbage collections, live. */ public class StreamingDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (RecordingStream rs = new RecordingStream()) { rs.enable("workbench.IssuerCall").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(35)); // only the slow ones rs.enable("jdk.GarbageCollection"); rs.onEvent("workbench.IssuerCall", e -> System.out.printf("slow issuer call: %s, %d ms%n", e.getString("merchant"), e.getDuration().toMillis())); rs.onEvent("jdk.GarbageCollection", e -> System.out.printf("GC: %s, %.1f ms pause total%n", e.getString("name"), e.getDuration("sumOfPauses").toNanos() / 1e6)); rs.startAsync(); // events arrive on a background thread PaymentWorkload.run(3); Thread.sleep(1_500); // let the last flush reach us } } }

alt.title: StreamingDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l05 import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingStream import java.time.Duration // Kotlin twin of StreamingDemo.java: slow issuer calls and garbage collections, live, from inside the JVM. fun main() { RecordingStream().use { rs -> rs.enable("workbench.IssuerCall").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(35)) // only the slow ones rs.enable("jdk.GarbageCollection") rs.onEvent("workbench.IssuerCall") { e -> println("slow issuer call: ${e.getString("merchant")}, ${e.duration.toMillis()} ms") } rs.onEvent("jdk.GarbageCollection") { e -> println("GC: %s, %.1f ms pause total".format(e.getString("name"), e.getDuration("sumOfPauses").toNanos() / 1e6)) } rs.startAsync() // events arrive on a background thread kRunWorkload(3) Thread.sleep(1_500) // let the last flush reach us } }

try.expect: Lines such as slow issuer call: m_7, 39 ms keep arriving in batches, mixed with GC: G1New, 1.5 ms pause total. Only m_7 appears, between 35 and 40 ms, because of the threshold and the fake issuer. For the JDK 25 step, run java '-XX:StartFlightRecording:method-timing=workbench.performance.l05.PaymentWorkload::fee,report-on-exit=method-timing' -cp performance/build/classes/java/demo workbench.performance.l05.JfrDemo child from labs/: it ends with a Method Timing table for fee.

analogy: JFR is the flight recorder in an aircraft. It's always on, records hundreds of instrument readings with timestamps, and costs little enough that nobody switches it off. When something goes wrong you pull the box and replay the minutes around it. Your custom events are the cockpit voice recorder: what the crew (your code) was doing, on the same clock as the instruments. The analogy breaks in one useful way: you can pull JFR's data from a running JVM with jcmd ... JFR.dump without stopping anything, and you can even subscribe to it live with RecordingStream.
world: Run your Quarkus payment services with a continuous recording using default.jfc, maxage and maxsize set so it keeps the last hour or so. When the authorization p99 jumps, jcmd <pid> JFR.dump gives you the minutes around it without a restart, and jfr view gc-pauses and contention-by-site tell you quickly whether the JVM is involved. Add one custom event around each issuer call and each Kafka batch, with merchant, partition and outcome as fields, so you can line them up with GC and lock events. Before a recording leaves your network, remember it contains environment variables and command-line arguments, and on JDK 27 use the redaction options.
mistake:
The common mistake is turning on profile.jfc in production "because more data is better", or starting a recording with no limits and never dumping it. profile doubles the sampling and lowers the lock thresholds, and the man page itself says it can have more overhead and belongs in short periods. A recording without maxage or maxsize falls back to a 250 MB default, so set limits that match how far back you need to look. The fix is a continuous default recording with limits, plus a short profile recording started with jcmd when you are investigating.

Java
// a continuous recording, started from code, keeping the last hour within 200 MB
Recording r = new Recording(Configuration.getConfiguration("default"));
r.setMaxAge(Duration.ofHours(1));
r.setMaxSize(200L * 1024 * 1024);
r.start();
Kotlin
// a continuous recording, started from code, keeping the last hour within 200 MB
val r = Recording(Configuration.getConfiguration("default"))
r.maxAge = Duration.ofHours(1)
r.maxSize = 200L * 1024 * 1024
r.start()

compare.title: A custom JFR event in Java and Kotlin

java.title: IssuerCallEvent.java
java.html: @Name("workbench.IssuerCall") @Label("Issuer Call") @Category({"Workbench", "Payments"}) public class IssuerCallEvent extends Event { @Label("Merchant") String merchant; @Label("Amount (cents)") long amountCents; @Label("Approved") boolean approved; } IssuerCallEvent event = new IssuerCallEvent(); event.begin(); // 1. start the clock boolean approved = issuer.approve(merchant, cents); event.end(); // 2. stop it if (event.shouldCommit()) { // 3. false if no recording wants it event.merchant = merchant; event.amountCents = cents; event.approved = approved; event.commit(); // 4. write it, with a stack trace }

kotlin.title: JfrDemo.kt
kotlin.html: @Name("workbench.IssuerCall") @Label("Issuer Call") @Category("Workbench", "Payments") class KIssuerCallEvent : Event() { @Label("Merchant") var merchant: String? = null @Label("Amount (cents)") var amountCents = 0L @Label("Approved") var approved = false } val event = KIssuerCallEvent() event.begin() // 1. start the clock val approved = issuer.approve(merchant, cents) event.end() // 2. stop it if (event.shouldCommit()) { // 3. false if no recording wants it event.merchant = merchant event.amountCents = cents event.approved = approved event.commit() // 4. write it, with a stack trace }

compare.note: The same event, recorded the same way. Kotlin properties work as event fields: a var compiles to a private field plus accessors, and JFR records the field. A Java annotation such as @Label placed on a Kotlin property goes to that field, because FIELD is the only one of its targets a property can use. @Category takes an array, written {"Workbench", "Payments"} in Java and as plain arguments in Kotlin. Both versions produce the same event type, workbench.IssuerCall, so the same jfr view works on either recording.

worked.title: Explain a latency spike with one dump

steps.say: Authorization p99 jumped at 14:02 on one pod. The pod runs a continuous recording. Dump the last 10 minutes without restarting anything.
steps.code: jcmd 4711 JFR.check jcmd 4711 JFR.dump name=1 maxage=10m filename=/tmp/auth-1402.jfr

steps.say: First question: did the JVM stop the world? gc-pauses answers in one screen. If the longest pause is a few ms, GC isn't your 200 ms.
Second question: did threads wait on each other? contention-by-site lists monitors that threads waited on, with counts and the longest wait. A 180 ms max on a ledger lock would explain a lot.

Third question: which calls were slow, and for whom? Your own event answers it, on the same clock. Self-check: if the slow issuer calls and a long lock wait share a thread name and a timestamp, which one do you look at first? (The lock wait: it's inside your process and the issuer call may only look slow because the thread was waiting.)
steps.code: jfr print --events workbench.IssuerCall /tmp/auth-1402.jfr | grep -B3 -A6 'duration = [0-9][0-9][0-9] ms'

steps.say: Write the finding down with the evidence, and attach the views, not the raw file: the file contains environment variables and arguments.

lab.title: Emit a custom event and read it back
steps: Run the tests. All five fail. Each test starts a real JFR recording, calls your Authorizer six times, dumps a real .jfr file and reads it back.
Make AuthorizationEvent an event named workbench.Authorization, with a label, a category that includes Payments, and three labelled fields: merchant, amountCents, approved.
In Authorizer.authorize, record one event per call. Its duration must cover the issuer call: one fake issuer takes 40 ms and the test checks for it.
Write AuthReport.declinesByMerchant and AuthReport.slowestMerchant with RecordingFile. The file also contains jdk.ThreadSleep events, so filter by event name.
Run the tests until all five pass. Then run JfrDemo again and try jfr view on your own recording.
hints: The annotations are @Name, @Label, @Category and @Description from jdk.jfr. The fields can stay package-private.
Call begin() right before the issuer call and end() right after it. Fill the fields and commit() inside if (event.shouldCommit()).
RecordingFile.readAllEvents(path) returns a List<RecordedEvent>. Filter on e.getEventType().getName(), then use e.getBoolean("approved"), e.getString("merchant") and e.getDuration().
Map.merge(merchant, 1L, Long::sum) counts per key in one line. A TreeMap keeps the result sorted, which makes failures easier to read.

drill.title: From memory: event, recording, query
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write (1) an event class LedgerWriteEvent named workbench.LedgerWrite with an account field, (2) the code that times a ledger write with it, and (3) the two shell commands that start a recording on JVM 4711 and later write it to ledger.jfr. Then check against the answer.

answer.html: @Name("workbench.LedgerWrite") @Label("Ledger Write") @Category({"Workbench", "Ledger"}) class LedgerWriteEvent extends Event { @Label("Account") String account; } LedgerWriteEvent event = new LedgerWriteEvent(); event.begin(); ledger.write(entry); event.end(); if (event.shouldCommit()) { event.account = entry.account(); event.commit(); } // jcmd 4711 JFR.start name=ledger settings=profile // jcmd 4711 JFR.dump name=ledger filename=ledger.jfr

alt.html: @Name("workbench.LedgerWrite") @Label("Ledger Write") @Category("Workbench", "Ledger") class LedgerWriteEvent : Event() { @Label("Account") var account: String? = null } val event = LedgerWriteEvent() event.begin() ledger.write(entry) event.end() if (event.shouldCommit()) { event.account = entry.account event.commit() } // jcmd 4711 JFR.start name=ledger settings=profile // jcmd 4711 JFR.dump name=ledger filename=ledger.jfr

recap: JFR is built into HotSpot and records timestamped events (GC, JIT, locks, CPU and allocation samples, I/O) on one timeline. Start it with -XX:StartFlightRecording or jcmd <pid> JFR.start, and copy data out with JFR.dump.
default.jfc is for leaving on; profile.jfc samples twice as often and lowers lock thresholds, so use it for short investigations. Set maxage or maxsize.
jfr summary shows what's in a file, jfr view (JDK 21+) prints reports such as hot-methods, allocation-by-site, gc-pauses and contention-by-site, and jfr print shows single events.
Custom events extend jdk.jfr.Event: begin, end, shouldCommit, commit. They share the timeline with the JVM's events. RecordingFile reads them back; RecordingStream delivers them live.
JDK 25 adds method timing (JEP 520), experimental CPU-time sampling on Linux (JEP 509) and report-on-exit. Recordings contain environment variables and arguments; JDK 27 can redact them.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why you'd add a JFR event around the issuer call when there's already a log line with the duration. Explain the difference in your own words.
explain.answer: The log line gives one number per call as text, and it's always on. A JFR event is structured: merchant, amount and outcome are fields I can filter and group without parsing. It costs almost nothing when no recording enables it, and a recording can keep only the slow ones with a threshold. Most importantly, it lands on the same timeline as the JVM's own events, so for a slow call I can see whether a GC pause, a lock wait or a burst of allocation happened on the same thread at the same moment. A log line can't tell me that.

deeper.html:
JFR's views are queries, and the JDK source keeps them in a file called view.ini. For example, hot-methods is SELECT stackTrace.topFrame AS T, COUNT(*), COUNT(*) FROM ExecutionSample GROUP BY T LIMIT 25, and deoptimizations-by-reason is SELECT reason, COUNT(reason) AS C FROM Deoptimization GROUP BY reason ORDER BY C DESC. jfr view --verbose shows which fields a view uses, which helps when you build your own analysis with RecordingFile.

The demo recorded only 28 execution samples in 4 seconds. Its threads sleep most of the time, and the classic sampler records threads that are running Java code, not sleeping ones. Even so, 28 is fewer than a 10 ms period suggests, and this course couldn't pin down the sampler's exact rules in the source. That's one reason lesson 6 brings in async-profiler, which samples with signals and timers, and JDK 25 brought the CPU-time sampler.

jfr has more subcommands: jfr configure builds a custom .jfc from options, jfr scrub writes a copy of a recording without chosen events, jfr assemble and jfr disassemble join and split chunk files, and jfr metadata lists every event type and field.

To record a whole test run in CI, add -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=build/test.jfr to the test JVM's arguments. On JDK 25, report-on-exit=allocation-by-site prints the allocation report straight into the build log.
